evidence.text: Hold four seconds of random letters and you’ll catch about seven. Hold four seconds of a sentence and you’ll catch far more, maybe fifty letters’ worth. The exposure is identical and the raw capacity never moved. The sentence just arrives pre-packed.

A student known as SF trained his digit span from an ordinary seven up to seventy-nine by learning to hear strings of numbers as running times he already knew from athletics. Then they tested him on letters. Six. The capacity never grew at all.

stories.text: This is the bridge to IQ. A span test measures how much you can hold before any training goes in. Expertise is defined by building learned shortcuts around exactly that limit. So the test aims squarely at the one thing expertise exists to get past, and then calls it the core of intelligence.

relations.justification: Chunks form as patterns become automatic.
Chunks only work in the domain where they were built, which is one reason intelligence is domain-specific.
Memory for digits and skill at logic both look like inborn capacities, and both turn out to be built through learning.

games.name: The Bottleneck
games.blurb: Remember strings of letters for four seconds, then find out why the same letters were easy or impossible depending on their order.

games.name: The Ayumu Test
games.blurb: Nine numbers flash for a fraction of a second and you try to tap them in order. A young chimpanzee will beat you, and the reason is training, not brains.

stations.bookRef: The book explains why IQ tests track basic resources like working memory, and why those resources matter far less than what we’ve learned.

next.reason: How much does your brain do without you noticing?

stations.contested: People with great memories were born with more capacity, and experts can hold more in their heads.

flow.chunk: How many random digits can you repeat back after hearing them read once? For most people, it’s about seven, and that’s only because we can repeat the digits to ourselves and group them. On its own, the conscious mind can hold only about four items at a time, a limit the book calls the conscious bottleneck.

flow.ask: In a famous study, an ordinary college student spent about 230 hours over twenty months practicing repeating back strings of random digits. He was a competitive runner, and he learned to hear groups of digits as running times, so “3492” became a single item: a near-record mile time of 3 minutes and 49.2 seconds. His digit span rose from seven to seventy-nine. Then the researchers tested him on random letters instead of digits. What do you think happened?
choices: His letter span was also around seventy-nine, because his memory had grown
His letter span was still about six, because his running-time method only worked on digits
His letter span landed somewhere in between
flow.answer:
His letter span was about six, the same as before he started. His memory capacity hadn’t grown at all. What he had built was a way of grouping digits into meaningful chunks, using running times he already knew. Each chunk took up one slot in his memory, so he could hold far more digits in the same small space.

That method only worked on digits. Letters don’t look like running times, so with letters he was back to one item per slot.

flow.chunk:
You did the same thing as the runner when you learned to read. At first, a letter was just a set of lines, and your conscious mind had to take them in one at a time. With practice, you built networks that recognize a whole letter as a single item, and then a whole word.

Now, when you look at a word like THINK, you take in all twelve of its lines at once. Your conscious mind still takes in one item at a time and holds only about four. What learning changes is how much each item contains.

flow.ask: Imagine a physicist whose working memory scores are in the top 5 percent, and who has never played chess. He plays a fifth-grader whose working memory and attention scores are below average for her age. She has played chess since she was five, and she ranks among the top three players her age in her state. Who wins?
choices: The physicist, because he can hold more in his head
The fifth-grader
It would be a close match
flow.answer:
The fifth-grader wins easily. She has spent years building chess patterns into her expert networks, so she recognizes familiar positions and good moves at a glance. The physicist has none of those patterns, so a larger working memory doesn’t help him.

Working memory is one of the brain’s basic resources. Resources help, but they can’t solve problems on their own. What solves problems is the skill you’ve built through learning.

flow.ask: IQ tests include tasks like repeating back strings of digits, and IQ scores are most closely linked to working memory. Given the runner and the young chess player, what do those scores mostly measure?
choices: How intelligent a person is across every area of life
Basic resources like working memory, which help with learning but aren’t intelligence
How hard a person tried on the day of the test
flow.answer:
IQ scores mostly reflect basic resources like working memory, which help with learning but aren’t intelligence. The runner shows how little those resources decide. With a learned pattern, his digit span went from seven to seventy-nine while his memory capacity stayed exactly the same.

Intelligence is your ability to solve problems in a given domain, and that ability is built through learning.

flow.ask: Here is the belief, then: people with great memories were born with more room in their heads. Does the runner’s letter span support that?
choices: Great memories come from a larger capacity people are born with
Great memories come from learned patterns that pack more into each item
Great memories come from a larger inborn capacity, plus practice
flow.answer:
The runner’s letter span shows the opposite. Great memories come from learning. The conscious bottleneck is small for everyone. Experts don’t have more room. What they have is learned patterns that let them treat a whole group of things as a single item.

That’s why an expert’s memory advantage disappears outside their field, the way the runner’s did when the digits turned into letters.

stations.name: Everyday Genius
stations.oneBreath: The skills you use without thinking, like walking across a room, understanding speech, and recognizing faces, are solutions to some of the most complex problems a brain ever faces. We don’t call them genius only because nearly everyone has them. The book calls this common genius.

claimsBlock.believe: Real intelligence is rare. Walking and talking are just basic things everybody can do.
claimsBlock.evidence: Easy does not mean simple. The feats we dismiss as basic are the most sophisticated things any mind does, and they run on the same machinery as everything we do call genius.

evidence.text: The things people find easiest turned out to be the hardest to program into a computer, and the things people find hardest turned out to be the easy ones. A mechanical device was cranking out valid logic in the 1860s. Walking across a cluttered room took the best minds in computing decades, and some of it still isn’t solved well.

Taking an IQ test requires understanding language, holding instructions in mind, recognizing shapes and controlling your attention. Every one of those prerequisites is more complex than the puzzles the test then scores you on. The hard part is the part we treat as a given.
evidence.cite: The prerequisites of a cognitive test

relations.justification: We underrate these skills because we can’t feel the work they require.
Celebrated genius is built by the same learning engine as walking and reading, on a less common path.
The fact that everyone has these skills shows that the capacity for genius is universal.

stations.bookRef: The book uses the term common genius for the extraordinary skills that nearly everyone has.

next.reason: What is intelligence, and why can’t it be ranked on one scale?

stations.contested: Real intelligence is rare. Walking and talking are basic skills anyone can do.

flow.chunk:
When computer scientists started trying to build thinking machines in the mid-twentieth century, they assumed that the problems humans find hardest, like chess and math, would be the hardest to program. Those turned out to be the easy ones. Pocket calculators have existed since the 1970s, and a computer beat the world chess champion in 1997.

What turned out to be hard were skills every toddler has, like walking across a cluttered room without falling and recognizing a face from any angle. Robots still struggle with tasks like folding laundry. This is known as Moravec’s Paradox.

flow.ask: Why would the skills that feel easiest to us turn out to be the hardest to program?
choices: Because computers are bad at anything physical
Because those skills are extremely complex, and they only feel easy because we’ve mastered them so completely
Because nobody tried hard enough to program them
flow.answer:
Because they solve some of the most complex problems a brain ever faces. They feel easy because we’ve automated them so completely that we don’t feel any of the work. As the book puts it, easy does not equal simple.

The computer scientists made the same mistake the rest of us make: they judged how complex a skill is by how hard it feels to do.

flow.ask: Think back to your first time behind the wheel, when talking while you drove was impossible. Now you’re driving home with an old friend in the passenger seat, and you talk the whole way. To pull that off, you’re tracking the cars around you, obeying traffic signals, and adjusting your speed, while also decoding speech, following the story, catching jokes, and choosing what to say. Productivity experts often say humans can’t multitask. How does that fit with your drive home?
choices: It fits. This isn’t really multitasking
It doesn’t fit. This is multitasking at a very high level, made possible by skills that run automatically
It only works because driving is easy
flow.answer:
This is multitasking at a very high level. It’s possible because both driving and conversation run in expert networks that don’t need your conscious attention. It took computer scientists decades to get machines to do even one of those things.

There was a time you couldn’t do either one. You built every one of those skills through learning.

flow.ask: Walking, talking, and recognizing faces solve some of the hardest problems a brain faces. So why doesn’t anyone call a toddler a genius?
choices: Because what toddlers do isn’t actually difficult
Because nearly every toddler can do it, so it isn’t rare
Because toddlers are born able to do it
flow.answer:
Because it isn’t rare. When we call something genius, we usually mean two things: it solved a very difficult problem, and few other people could have done it. Walking, talking, and recognizing faces easily pass the first test. They fail only the second, because nearly everyone can do them.

If only one person on earth could talk or recognize faces, we would call that person a genius. The book calls these skills common genius.

flow.ask: Real intelligence, the thinking goes, is rare, and walking and talking are basic skills anyone can do. Which view fits Moravec’s Paradox and the drive home?
choices: Intelligence shows up only in rare achievements like chess and advanced math
The everyday skills everyone has are some of the most intelligent things a brain does
Everyday skills are complex, but they don’t count as intelligence
flow.answer: The everyday skills everyone has are some of the most intelligent things a brain does. They solve extraordinarily difficult problems, and they were built by the same learning process that produces every achievement we call genius.

stations.name: Uncommon Genius
stations.oneBreath: The breakthroughs we celebrate come from the same learning process that built your everyday skills. What makes them uncommon is the learning path. Someone spends years following an unusual curiosity, builds an unusual set of skills, and reaches solutions nobody else could.

claimsBlock.believe: Genius requires a special brain. Most people simply do not have what it takes.
claimsBlock.evidence: Uncommon interests build uncommon skills, and uncommon skills reach uncommon answers. The rarity is in the path, not the hardware.

evidence.text: Ten thousand hours pointed at chess builds a mind that sees a board in a way no untrained mind can. The hardware was standard issue. The ten thousand hours were not. Point those hours somewhere nobody else is pointing them and you get answers nobody else can reach.

stories.text: It stays rare for a sad reason. The Special Brain Story stops most people before they start. If you believe genius is something you’re issued at birth, you never put in the training that would have built it, and the belief never gets tested.

relations.justification: Common genius and uncommon genius are built by the same learning process. The difference is how unusual the learning path was.
The Special Brain Story stops people before they follow an unusual curiosity far enough to build uncommon skills.
An unusual learning path builds an unusual solution space.

stations.bookRef: The book argues that what we call genius comes from a learning path, and uses Einstein’s life as its central example.

next.reason: How does your brain use what it has learned to predict what comes next?

stations.contested: Genius requires a special brain, and most people don’t have what it takes.

flow.chunk:
Albert Einstein didn’t start speaking until around age two, and his parents and teachers worried about his speech for much of his childhood. Some of his teachers found him slow and dreamy, and he hated the rote drilling of his schools.

What he did have was curiosity. When he was five, his father showed him a compass, and he became fascinated by the invisible force that always pointed the needle north. He spent years thinking about the nature of light. At twenty-three, after failing to land a university job, he took an undemanding job as a patent clerk, which left him time to think about those questions every day.

flow.ask: Einstein spent those years reading papers, talking with other physicists, and working through thought experiments, and all of it built skills in his brain. The questions he was working on were ones almost nobody else was asking. What would you expect that path to produce?
choices: The same skills other physicists of his time had
An unusual set of skills, able to solve problems nobody else could
Very little, because unusual paths rarely lead anywhere
flow.answer:
An unusual set of skills. Because his learning path was unique, the set of problems his brain could solve was unique too. His discoveries only came within reach after that learning had been done. Before then, they were impossible for his brain, as they would be for anyone’s.

The book puts it this way: what separates uncommon genius from common genius is uniqueness, not complexity.

flow.ask: When plague closed Cambridge in 1665, Isaac Newton, then twenty-two, went home to his family’s farm, studied on his own, and invented calculus. Charles Darwin dropped out of medical school and spent five years on a ship collecting specimens. Emily Dickinson barely left her house for decades, and invented a new form of poetry. What do these three have in common?
choices: Each of them had an unusually powerful brain
Each of them followed their own curiosity down a path few others took
Each of them had excellent schooling
flow.answer:
Each of them followed their own curiosity. That created an unusual learning path, and an unusual learning path builds an unusual set of skills.

Many of the people we call geniuses learned this way, outside the schools and institutions of their time. What they have in common is how they learned.

flow.ask: What about child prodigies, like a five-year-old who plays chess at a very high level? Doesn’t that prove some brains are special from the start?
choices: Yes. Prodigies are born with special brains
No. What’s unusual about a prodigy is their interest, and the practice it leads to
No. Prodigies are just lucky
flow.answer:
A prodigy’s brain isn’t what’s unusual. What’s unusual is their interests. A five-year-old obsessed with chess instead of Pokémon is rare, and that obsession leads to thousands of hours of chess while other children are building different skills.

That’s why prodigies seem miraculous compared with other five-year-olds, but not compared with people who’ve had the same amount of practice.

flow.ask: The Special Brain Story says that genius requires a special brain, and that most people don’t have what it takes. Think about what Einstein, Newton, Darwin, and Dickinson had in common. Where did their genius come from?
choices: Their genius came from special brains, and the unusual paths were a side effect
Their genius came from unusual learning paths, built by the same learning process everyone has
Their genius came from special brains plus hard work
flow.answer: Their genius came from where their curiosity led them. The learning process that built your everyday skills is the same one that built Einstein’s discoveries. What made his work uncommon was the path his curiosity took, and the unique set of skills that path built.

stations.name: Domain-Specific Intelligence
stations.oneBreath: Intelligence is the ability to solve problems to reach your goals, and it’s always specific to the problems you’ve learned to solve. There’s no general quality that makes a person smart at everything, and no single scale that ranks people from least to most intelligent.

claimsBlock.believe: Smart is smart. A genius in one field is generally a sharp person across the board.
claimsBlock.evidence: Intelligence is contextual. It only makes sense in relation to specific problems and specific goals, and training in one domain barely helps in another.

evidence.text: Training in one domain barely helps in another. Chess training does not raise your math scores. Brain-training games make you better at brain-training games and very little else. If intelligence were one general resource, that is not what we would find.

We keep being surprised when a brilliant physicist is hopeless outside physics, or a chess champion can’t manage his own life, or Newton loses a fortune in a market bubble. The surprise is the giveaway. Those cases are baffling under one picture of intelligence and entirely expected under the other.
evidence.cite: The recurring surprise; Fischer, Newton, and others

stories.text: Put a world-class basketball player with no tennis experience against a well-trained fourth-grader, and the child wins. Every physical advantage the athlete has is real, and none of it matters, because tennis is a trained skill and the athlete hasn’t trained it.

relations.justification: Chunks only work in the domain where they were built.
Even reasoning, the ability that seems most general, turns out to be specific to what we’ve learned.
If there’s no general intelligence, there’s no generally superior brain.

stations.bookRef: The book defines intelligence as the ability to solve problems to reach your goals, and shows why that ability is always specific to a domain.

next.reason: Where do the achievements we call genius come from?

stations.contested: Smart is smart. Someone brilliant in one field is sharp across the board.

flow.ask: Jack and Jill both run out of toothpaste. Jill drives to the nearest drugstore and is home in twenty minutes. Jack drives around, turning wherever he feels like it, finds a store ninety minutes later, gets lost on the way back, and gets home five hours after he left. Both came home with toothpaste. Whose behavior was more intelligent?
choices: Neither, since both got the toothpaste
Jill’s, because she solved the problem far more efficiently
Jack’s, because he explored more
flow.answer: Jill’s. Both of them reached the goal, but Jill’s solution used far less time, gas, and effort. That’s what intelligence is: how well you solve problems to reach your goals. More effective and more efficient solutions demonstrate more intelligence.

flow.ask: Humans are far better than bats at sharing thoughts through spoken language. Bats are far better than humans at navigating a dark cave by echolocation. So which is more intelligent?
choices: Humans, because language is the harder problem
Bats, because echolocation is the harder problem
Neither. Each is more intelligent at its own problems
flow.answer:
Neither. Humans are more intelligent at sharing thoughts, and bats are more intelligent at navigating in the dark. Intelligence isn’t one general quality that a person or a species has more or less of across the board.

As the book puts it, asking whether one species is more intelligent than another is like asking whether a submarine is better at “transportation” than a helicopter.

flow.ask: IQ reduces intelligence to a single number meant to rank everyone from least to most intelligent. Given the bats and the humans, what’s the problem with that?
choices: There’s no problem. A single number is a fair summary
Intelligence depends on the problem being solved, so no single number can capture it
The number just needs to be measured more carefully
flow.answer:
The problem is that intelligence depends on the problem being solved, so it can’t be reduced to one score, any more than you can rank a submarine and a helicopter on a single scale. An IQ score reflects how well someone solves the particular kinds of problems on the test, at the time they take it.

Humans are also the only animals who could score well on an IQ test, because we designed the test around the kinds of problems humans are good at. A bat would fail it, even though bats solve problems no human can.

flow.ask: We assume that someone brilliant in one field will be sharp in every field. Think of the physicist from The Bottleneck and Chunking station, who lost at chess to a fifth-grader. Think of the bats and the humans, each far better at its own problems. Does brilliance carry over from one field to another?
choices: Brilliance carries over. A brilliant person is sharp in every field
Brilliance stays in the field where it was built
Brilliance mostly carries over, with a few exceptions
flow.answer:
Brilliance stays in the field where it was built. The physicist’s years of physics did nothing for him at the chessboard. Intelligence is always specific to a domain, and it’s built by learning in that domain. An expert in one field is a beginner in every field they haven’t studied.

That’s why we’re so often surprised when a brilliant scientist makes poor decisions about money, or a chess champion struggles to run their own life. Those cases are exactly what you’d expect when intelligence is built one domain at a time.

stations.name: The Prediction Engine
stations.oneBreath: Your brain doesn’t just take in what’s happening and then react to it. It constantly predicts what’s about to happen, based on everything it has learned, and checks those predictions against what actually happens. Much of what we call skill is prediction built through learning.

evidence.text: Give someone a sentence they’ve never seen and they can guess the next word fast and often get it right. That only works one way. The brain has to be running ahead of the words the whole time, generating what’s likely and standing ready for it.

A language model built by Anthropic learned everything it can do from training alone, by predicting the next piece of text over and over until capability fell out of the practice. It’s an odd sort of proof of this whole map. Capability built from training, in a computer, working from a rough copy of this one part of you.
evidence.cite: Large language models as trained prediction

relations.justification: Wrong predictions produce the error signals that drive learning.
Predictions only work in the domain where they were learned.

stations.bookRef: The book describes pattern recognition as the brain’s core competency.

next.reason: Why can’t you always reach what you know?

stations.contested: My brain takes in the world first, and then figures out what it means.

flow.ask: Read this sentence: “She opened her umbrella because it had started to ___.” Before you reached the blank, you probably already knew what word was coming. How could you know?
choices: Because you had read that exact sentence before
Because your brain was predicting the next word, based on patterns it has learned
Because you read ahead to the end of the line
flow.answer:
Your brain was predicting the next word. It uses the patterns it has learned from years of reading and listening to prepare for what’s likely to come next.

That’s a big part of why reading and listening feel effortless, and why you can often finish someone else’s sentence.

flow.ask: Albert Pujols, one of the best hitters in baseball history, regularly hit fastballs thrown at over 90 miles per hour. In a 2004 exhibition, he faced the Olympic softball pitcher Jennie Finch, who throws underhand, and he couldn’t make contact. When researchers tested his reaction time, it was only a little above average for a college student. So what made him such a great hitter?
choices: Faster reflexes than other people
Years of learning to predict where a pitch was going from the pitcher’s motion
Better eyesight
flow.answer:
Years of learning to predict. A fastball reaches the plate in about four-tenths of a second, too fast to wait and see where it’s going, so hitters start their swing based on what the pitcher’s body and the ball’s first few feet of flight tell them. Pujols had spent years building that prediction skill against baseball pitchers.

Finch’s underhand motion looked nothing like what he had trained on, so his predictions didn’t work, and his skill didn’t carry over. Much of what looks like fast reflexes is prediction built through learning, and it only works in the domain where it was built.

flow.ask: You’re walking up a staircase in the dark, and you step for one more stair that isn’t there. What happens?
choices: Nothing. You just keep walking
You feel a jolt, because your brain had predicted a step
You fall down
flow.answer:
You feel a jolt. Your brain had predicted another step and had already prepared your leg for it. When the prediction turns out to be wrong, your brain registers the error instantly.

Those errors are how your brain learns. Each time a prediction fails, your brain uses the difference between what it expected and what happened to improve the next prediction.

flow.ask: It feels as if your brain takes in the world first and then works out what it means. In the umbrella sentence, the pitch, and the missing stair, which came first?
choices: Taking in the world came first, and working out what it meant came after
Prediction came first. Your brain prepared for what was likely before it happened
Prediction came first only for the expert hitter
flow.answer: Prediction came first. Your brain is constantly predicting what’s about to happen, based on what it has learned, and correcting itself when it’s wrong. Understanding a sentence, hitting a ball, and climbing stairs all depend on predictions built through learning.

stations.name: Routing Architecture
stations.oneBreath: Your brain operates in different modes, like focused work, mind-wandering, and sleep. Each mode changes which parts of the brain can communicate. The book calls the pattern of connections in each mode its routing architecture. Changing modes changes what you can reach, without changing anything you know.

evidence.text: The answer that wouldn’t come at your desk arrives in the shower, and nothing new was learned in between. The word you couldn’t find at dinner turns up the next morning without being asked. Same knowledge, different mode, different reach.

Under real pressure an expert can lose access to skills they’ve owned for years, and get them all back the moment the pressure lifts. The knowledge is provably still there a minute later. What high arousal did was change the routing, turning self-monitoring up and the automatic expert machinery down, which is the exact wrong mix for a practiced skill.

stories.text: Think of a smartphone. Only some of the apps are open at any moment, and only some of the open ones can pass information to each other. What the phone can do right now has very little to do with what’s installed on it.

relations.justification: Routing determines access, one of the two things that decide what you can do at a given moment.
Learning expands your solution space, and shifting your brain’s mode lets you reach more of what’s already in it.
Pressure and anxiety shift your routing in ways that block access to your skills.

stations.bookRef: The book devotes two chapters to routing: how the brain shifts between modes, and how to shift modes on purpose.

next.reason: What are the two things that determine what you can do at any moment?

stations.contested: If I can’t come up with something, I don’t really know it. And the way to find an answer is to keep trying harder.

flow.chunk:
For years, the chemist Dmitri Mendeleev tried to work out how the chemical elements were related. On long train rides, he wrote each element on a card and tried arranging the cards so that a pattern would appear. It never did.

According to the story he later told, he fell asleep at his desk one day after obsessing over the problem for days. In a dream, he saw a table where all the elements fell into place. When he woke up, he wrote it down. It became the periodic table.
flow.cite: Mendeleev, as told by Oliver Sacks

flow.ask: Mendeleev didn’t learn anything new while he was asleep. So how could his sleeping brain find something his waking brain couldn’t?
choices: He was consciously working on the problem in his dream
Sleep let parts of his brain connect that couldn’t while he was awake
It was a lucky guess
flow.answer:
Sleep changed how information flowed through his brain. Mendeleev had spent years building the knowledge he needed. What he still needed was to connect that knowledge in a new way, and the pattern of brain activity during sleep made those connections possible. The sleepers in the number-puzzle study from the Capability-Accessibility Model station showed the same thing. Sleep didn’t change what they knew. It changed what they could get to.

The book calls each of these patterns of brain activity a routing architecture. Each mode your brain operates in, from focused work to sleep, has its own routing architecture.

flow.chunk:
The book compares this to a subway system. During the day, one set of stations and tracks is open. At night, a different set opens, and you can reach places you couldn’t get to during the day.

Your brain works the same way. Focused work, mind-wandering, and sleep each open some routes between brain regions and close others. The knowledge in your brain stays the same. What changes is which parts of it can connect.

flow.ask: In one study, people spent a few minutes listing unusual uses for everyday objects, like a brick. Then they took a break. Some spent it on a demanding task, and others did an easy task that let their minds wander. When they came back to the same objects, the mind-wanderers came up with far more new uses. Why?
choices: The easy task left them less tired
Mind-wandering put their brains in a mode that could reach different ideas
The easy task gave them more time to think about the objects
flow.answer:
Mind-wandering shifted their brains into a different mode, called the default mode, which has its own routing architecture. That mode connected ideas that stayed apart while they were focused.

It wasn’t rest alone. A third group that simply rested during the break didn’t improve. It’s the same reason a name you couldn’t remember comes to you later, once you’ve stopped trying.

flow.ask: An expert performer under intense pressure suddenly can’t do something they’ve done thousands of times. An hour later, the skill is back. Given what we’ve reviewed, what did the pressure do?
choices: The pressure erased the skill for a while
The pressure shifted the brain into a mode that blocked access to the skill
The pressure revealed that the skill was never solid
flow.answer:
It shifted the brain into a different mode. Under pressure, the parts of the brain that monitor and judge you become more active, and they interfere with the expert networks that normally run the skill on their own.

This is the same thing that happens when your mind goes blank during a toast. The skill was in the performer’s brain the whole time, but the brain state they were in couldn’t reach it.

flow.ask: We tend to think that if we can’t come up with something, we don’t really know it, and that the way to find an answer is to keep trying harder. Given Mendeleev and the mind-wanderers, is trying harder the way to find an answer?
choices: Trying harder works. If you know something, enough effort will bring it out
Trying harder can keep you stuck. Sometimes stepping away is what makes the answer reachable
Trying harder works as long as you’ve studied enough
flow.answer:
Trying harder can keep you stuck. What you can do at any moment depends on what you’ve learned and on the mode your brain is in, because each mode gives you access to a different part of what you know. Trying harder keeps your brain in the focused mode. Stepping away, resting, or sleeping can shift it into a mode that reaches the answer.

Many of history’s most productive thinkers built mode shifts into their days. Charles Darwin spent a few focused hours at his desk each morning, then walked his gravel “thinking path.” Beethoven walked for hours in nature, where ideas for his compositions often came to him.

stations.name: Solution Space
stations.oneBreath: Your solution space is the set of problems you can currently solve. The book pictures it as land inside a fence. Learning moves the fence outward, and shifting your brain’s mode lets you reach more of the land inside it.

evidence.text: Walking across your bedroom is inside your solution space. Playing a Rachmaninoff concerto is outside it, and the only thing that would ever bring it inside is years of learning. That’s the first door, and it adds skills permanently, a layer at a time.
evidence.cite: The two paths to a larger solution space

relations.justification: Learning adds to your solution space one skill at a time, each built on the ones before it.
Shifting your brain’s mode lets you reach parts of your solution space that were out of reach.
What you can do right now depends on your solution space and how much of it you can access.

stations.bookRef: The book describes your solution space as the land you’ve fenced off so far, and learning as moving the fence posts outward.

next.reason: What built your solution space in the first place?

stations.contested: What I’m capable of is fixed by who I am.

flow.chunk:
The book describes everything you can currently do as a piece of land surrounded by a fence. Everything inside the fence is your solution space: the problems you’ve already learned to solve.

Reading this sentence is inside the fence. So are walking across your bedroom, making toast, and telling a bus from a bicycle. Playing Rachmaninoff’s Third Piano Concerto is probably outside it.

flow.ask: If you wanted to bring the Rachmaninoff concerto inside your fence, what would it take?
choices: A different brain
Years of learning to play the piano
Believing you can do it
flow.answer:
Years of learning to play the piano. The skills needed to play that concerto don’t exist in your brain yet, so for now it’s outside the fence, as it would be for anyone who hasn’t learned to play.

Learning is the only way to move the fence outward.

flow.ask: Your fence marks the problems you can solve today. What does it tell you about what you’re capable of learning?
choices: The fence shows the limit of what you’ll ever be able to learn
The fence tells you nothing about what you can learn. It shows where your learning has brought you so far
The fence shows how much natural talent you have
flow.answer:
It tells you nothing about that. It shows where your learning has brought you so far, not how far it can go.

The Impostor looks at that fence and sees a concrete wall, fixed at birth by your genes. That’s the Special Brain Story. The Genius built the fence through learning, and more learning moves it.

flow.chunk:
Moving the fence isn’t the only way to do more. In the sleep study from the Capability-Accessibility Model station, the sleepers found a hidden shortcut without being taught anything new. The shortcut was inside their fence all along. Sleep shifted their brains into a mode that could reach it.

At any given moment, your brain can reach only part of your solution space, depending on the mode it’s in.

flow.ask: Many people believe that what they can do is fixed by who they are. What do the fence and the sleep study say?
choices: Capability is fixed. Some things are beyond certain people
Capability changes. It depends on what you’ve learned and what you can access, and both can change
Capability grows with learning, but only up to a point
flow.answer: What you’re capable of isn’t fixed. It depends on two things you can change: what you’ve learned, and what your brain can access in its current mode. Learning moves the fence outward. Shifting modes lets you reach more of the land inside it.

stations.name: The Unreliable Narrator
stations.oneBreath: The part of your brain that explains your choices often doesn’t have access to the real reasons for them. It produces a believable story, and you believe it too. The same narrator also tells you what you can and can’t do, and it’s just as unreliable about that.

evidence.text: Give people a themed list of words, say bed, rest, tired and dream, and a great many of them will later swear that sleep was on the list. Often with more confidence than they have about the words that actually were. The brain rebuilt the theme so smoothly that it supplied the missing centerpiece and stamped it as genuine.

stories.text: The line I have always been bad at math runs on this exact machinery. It feels like a fact recalled from a lifetime of evidence. It is a story, rebuilt from a handful of old moments and smoothed into a certainty that then goes looking for confirmation and finds it everywhere.

relations.justification: The narrator’s confident, unreliable explanations are how the Impostor speaks.
The narrator’s stories about what you can’t do support the Special Brain Story.

stations.bookRef: This station follows the book’s chapter “An Unreliable Narrator.”

next.reason: What is the most damaging story the narrator tells?

stations.contested: I know why I do what I do, and I know what I’m capable of.

flow.chunk:
Researchers reviewed more than a thousand parole decisions made by eight judges in Israel over ten months. The chance that a prisoner would be granted parole didn’t depend much on the severity of the crime or on the prisoner’s record.

It depended on how long it had been since the judge’s last meal break. Right after a break, prisoners had about a 65 percent chance of parole. By the end of a long session without one, that chance had fallen close to zero.

flow.ask: If you had asked those judges why they made each decision, what do you think they would have said?
choices: That they were hungry or tired
That each decision was based on the facts of the case
That they didn’t know
flow.answer:
They would have explained each decision using the facts of the case, and they would have believed it. Nothing in their explanations would have mentioned how long it had been since their last break.

Whatever was driving the pattern, whether hunger or mental fatigue, was outside their awareness, so it never appeared in their explanations.

flow.ask: In another study, people looked at one pair of photos after another and picked the face they found more attractive. Then the researcher secretly swapped the photos and asked them to explain their choice while showing them the face they had rejected. The switch was caught only about one time in four. The rest of the time, people explained in detail why they had chosen a face they hadn’t chosen, saying things like “she has kind eyes.” What does that tell you about where our explanations come from?
choices: The people were lying to please the researcher
The part of the brain that explains our choices doesn’t know why we made them, so it builds a believable story
The people had poor eyesight
flow.answer:
It tells you that the part of the brain that explains our choices doesn’t have access to the real reasons. Its job is to produce an explanation that sounds right to other people, and it does that whether or not it knows the truth.

The made-up explanations were just as detailed and heartfelt as the ones people gave for their real choices. So feeling sure of our reasons tells us very little about whether they’re true.

flow.ask: Dennis, the patient from the Capability-Accessibility Model station, insisted he couldn’t recognize written words after his stroke. His doctor handed him cards with the names of plants and animals and asked him to sort them into two piles with his left hand, as fast as he could. He sorted all but one correctly. The chance of doing that by guessing was less than 1 in 4,000. What does that tell you?
choices: He had been pretending he couldn’t read
Part of his brain could still recognize the words, but the part that talks didn’t know it
He got lucky
flow.answer:
The right side of Dennis’s brain, which controls the left hand, was still receiving what his eyes saw, and it could read the words well enough to guide that hand. But that information never reached the part of his brain that talks. So he honestly believed he couldn’t do it, and he was as surprised by the result as everyone else in the room.

The narrator in your head can be wrong about what you’re capable of, not only about why you do things.

flow.ask: We tend to think that we know why we do what we do, and that we know what we’re capable of. What do the judges, the swapped photos, and Dennis say about that?
choices: We know our own reasons and abilities, because we have direct access to them
The voice that explains us often doesn’t know the real reasons, or everything we can do
We know our reasons, except when the stakes are high
flow.answer:
The voice that explains you often doesn’t know the real causes. It tells a story about your choices and your abilities either way. The book calls that voice the Impostor.

Its stories about what you can’t do are no more reliable than its stories about why you picked a face.

stations.name: Trained Reasoning
stations.oneBreath: Reasoning feels like a general ability you can apply to anything. But the same logic problem can be easy in one form and nearly impossible in another. Reasoning depends on the patterns you’ve learned, which makes it a skill like any other, built through learning.

claimsBlock.believe: Reasoning is a general faculty. Either you are a logical person or you are not.
claimsBlock.evidence: Reasoning is a trained skill rather than a general faculty. Change the wording and performance collapses or soars, which a genuine logic engine could not do.

evidence.text: You have probably heard that the mind runs in two gears, a fast automatic one and a slow careful reasoner that does the real thinking. Test the second gear on an abstract logic puzzle and fewer than one person in ten gets it right, however long you give them.
evidence.cite: Reasoning as a built skill, not an innate faculty

evidence.text: There’s a famous logic puzzle that almost everyone fails when it’s about letters and numbers on cards. Dress the identical puzzle up as a bartender checking who is old enough to drink and almost everyone gets it. Same logic, same structure, different wording. A general logic engine could not behave that way.
evidence.cite: The Wason selection task, abstract versus social versions

evidence.text: The same problem is easy as a count of people and hard as a percentage, easy as a story and hard as a formula. Ask doctors about a medical test in percentages and most get it badly wrong. Ask them the identical question as a count of people out of a thousand and most get it right.
evidence.cite: Framing and frequency effects in reasoning

stories.text: The hopeful part is that this cuts both ways. Because reasoning is a trained skill rather than a fixed trait, you can teach it. Show someone how to turn the hard wording into the easy one and their score climbs on the very next round, in minutes, with no new brain required.

relations.justification: Reasoning is the ability that seems most general, which makes it the strongest example of intelligence being domain-specific.
Logic puzzles show the same thing as the runner’s digit memory: an ability that seems inborn depends on patterns built through learning.
We assumed reasoning was a general ability because effortful thinking is the part of the mind we can feel.

stations.bookRef: The book argues that thinking skills like logic and math are built by the same learning process as walking and talking.

next.reason: What story ties all of these mistaken beliefs together?

stations.contested: Reasoning is a general ability. Some people are logical and others aren’t.

flow.ask: Here’s a famous logic puzzle. Four cards lie on a table, showing A, D, 4, and 7. Each card has a letter on one side and a number on the other. The rule is: if a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other side. Which cards do you need to turn over to check whether the rule is being followed?
choices: A and 4
A and 7
A only
All four cards
flow.answer:
A and 7. If the A has an odd number on the back, the rule is broken. If the 7 has a vowel on the back, the rule is broken too. The 4 doesn’t matter, because the rule says nothing about what must be on the back of an even number.

Most people choose A and 4. In study after study, fewer than one in ten people get this right.

flow.ask: Now try the same puzzle in a different form. You’re a bartender checking a rule: if someone is drinking beer, they must be over 21. Four people are at the bar. One is drinking beer, one is drinking soda, one is 25, and one is 16. Whose drink or age do you need to check?
choices: The beer drinker and the 16-year-old
The beer drinker and the 25-year-old
Everyone at the bar
flow.answer:
The beer drinker and the 16-year-old. Most people get this version right almost immediately. In studies, about three out of four people solve it.

It’s the same logical structure as the card puzzle. The beer drinker is the A, and the 16-year-old is the 7.

flow.ask: The logic of the two puzzles is identical. So why is one so much easier than the other?
choices: The letters and numbers in the card puzzle are confusing to look at
We’ve learned patterns for situations like checking who’s allowed to drink, but not for abstract letters and numbers
People try harder on the bar puzzle
flow.answer: Because reasoning depends on patterns we’ve learned in specific situations. Most adults have plenty of experience with rules about who’s allowed to do what, so the bar puzzle matches patterns their brains have already built. Abstract letters and numbers match nothing they’ve learned, so they have to work the problem out slowly with the conscious mind, where most people get it wrong.

flow.ask: The card puzzle felt like hard, careful thinking. The bar puzzle felt easy. We usually treat slow, effortful reasoning as the highest form of thinking. Given what you’ve just seen, what is that effort a sign of?
choices: That you’re using your intelligence at full power
That you’ve run into a problem your brain hasn’t built the patterns to solve yet
That the problem is impossible
flow.answer:
It’s a sign that you’ve run into a problem your brain hasn’t built the patterns for yet. Effortful reasoning is what happens when the conscious mind has to handle a problem on its own, because no expert network is available to do it.

With practice, those patterns get built, and the same kind of problem starts to feel easy. That’s also why formal logic has to be learned step by step, like any other skill.

flow.ask: The common view is that reasoning is a general ability, and some people are logical and others aren’t. The same people found identical logic hard in one form and easy in another. Knowing that, what’s the reality?
choices: Reasoning is a general ability. Logical people can reason well about anything
Reasoning is built from learned patterns, like every other skill, and it can be trained
Some people are born more logical, and training helps a little
flow.answer: Reasoning is a skill, built by the same learning process as walking, reading, and everything else you do. It depends on the patterns you’ve learned, which is why the same people found identical logic easy in one form and hard in another.
